magnesium-oxide.nameTh: แมกนีเซียมออกไซด์
magnesium-oxide.shortDescription: Magnesium oxide is a compound of magnesium and oxygen with a high proportion of elemental magnesium, which is why it is widely used as a mineral source in dietary supplements. Magnesium is an essential nutrient that plays a role in muscle function, the nervous system, bone structure and energy-yielding processes within cells.
magnesium-oxide.fullDescription:
Magnesium oxide, or MgO, is an inorganic compound formed from the elements magnesium and oxygen. It is a white powder, and elemental magnesium makes up approximately 60% of the weight of the pure compound. Because of this property, it is one of the forms of magnesium most commonly used as a raw material in dietary supplements.

Magnesium is involved in the activity of more than 300 enzyme systems in the body, ranging from protein synthesis and the production and use of energy to signalling between nerve cells and the regulation of muscle function. In addition, approximately 50–60% of the body's total magnesium is found in bone, with most of the remainder in muscle and soft tissue, reflecting the importance of this mineral for both the structure and the function of the body.
magnesium-oxide.howItWorks:
Magnesium and its mechanisms in the body
1. Muscle contraction and relaxation
Every movement of the body, from walking and exercising to the beating of the heart, involves several minerals working together. Magnesium works alongside calcium and potassium in regulating the movement of ions across cell membranes, which is an essential part of the process of muscle contraction and relaxation.
2. The nervous system and electrical signalling
Nerve cells use electrical signals and neurotransmitters to transmit information between the brain and different parts of the body. Magnesium is involved in regulating ion channels and the activity of certain neural receptors, which are fundamental mechanisms of communication within the nervous system.
3. Energy production and use at the cellular level
Most of the energy that cells use for their various activities is in the form of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). ATP is usually bound to a magnesium ion in the form of Mg-ATP so that enzymes can use its energy in biochemical reactions. Magnesium is therefore a key component of energy use at the cellular level.
4. Bone structure and mineral balance
In addition to calcium and phosphorus, magnesium is a mineral found in bone structure and is involved in regulating calcium balance, as well as in biochemical processes related to vitamin D. This reflects the fact that the maintenance of normal bones does not depend on any single nutrient alone.
magnesium-oxide.uniqueProperties:
How does magnesium oxide differ from other forms of magnesium?
| Form of magnesium | Key characteristics |
| Magnesium Oxide | High proportion of elemental magnesium, but low water solubility and lower absorption than some other forms |
| Magnesium Citrate | Magnesium bound to citric acid; generally better absorbed than magnesium oxide |
| Magnesium Glycinate | Magnesium bound to the amino acid glycine; direct comparative absorption data are still limited |
| Magnesium Chloride | A highly water-soluble magnesium compound with fairly good absorption |
| Magnesium Lactate | Magnesium bound to lactate; another form with supporting absorption data |
Food sources of magnesium
• Nuts and seeds, such as pumpkin seeds, almonds and cashews
• Green leafy vegetables, such as spinach, kale and chard
• Whole grains, such as brown rice, oats and wholewheat bread
• Legumes, such as black beans, red kidney beans, soybeans and chickpeas
• Other foods, such as dark chocolate, avocado, milk and yoghurt
• Dietary supplements, both as a single mineral and in formulas combined with other vitamins or minerals
magnesium-oxide.scientificEvidence:
1. Magnesium oxide and absorption
A 2019 study examined magnesium absorption in 14 healthy male volunteers, comparing magnesium oxide with magnesium citrate using blood and urine magnesium levels as indicators after ingestion.
The study found that magnesium citrate was better absorbed than magnesium oxide, indicating that chemical form is one of the factors affecting mineral absorption. However, this study had a relatively small number of participants and assessed outcomes only over the short term.
2. Magnesium, muscle function and cramps
A 2020 Cochrane systematic review pooled 11 trials with a total of 735 participants to evaluate the effect of magnesium supplementation on muscle cramps in several populations.
The review found that magnesium supplementation is unlikely to provide a clinically meaningful benefit for preventing cramps in older adults in general, while the evidence in pregnant women remains inconsistent. Although magnesium is essential for muscle function, additional magnesium intake does not mean it will help reduce cramps in every case.
3. Magnesium and bone mineral density
Information from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) states that magnesium is involved in bone formation and in regulating hormones that affect calcium balance, and several observational studies have found an association between dietary magnesium intake and bone mineral density.
However, this association cannot yet confirm that supplementation with magnesium oxide specifically will help increase bone mineral density or reduce the risk of fractures, so further clinical studies are still needed.
*This information is provided to educate about magnesium oxide and is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating any disease.
magnesium-oxide.safetyInformation:
Taking high amounts of magnesium may cause loose stools, nausea or stomach discomfort.
People with impaired kidney function should consult a doctor before taking dietary supplements containing magnesium, as the kidneys play a role in excreting excess magnesium from the body.
Magnesium may interfere with the absorption of certain antibiotics, such as tetracyclines and quinolones, as well as bisphosphonates, so consult a doctor or pharmacist about appropriate timing of intake.
keyFunctions: Magnesium contributes to normal functioning of the nervous system and muscles
Magnesium contributes to normal energy-yielding metabolism
Magnesium contributes to electrolyte balance
Magnesium contributes to the maintenance of normal bones
Magnesium contributes to the maintenance of normal teeth
Magnesium contributes to normal protein synthesis

oyster.shortDescription: Oysters are a seafood rich in a variety of nutrients, especially zinc, vitamin B12, iron and other minerals, which play an important part in immune function, protein building, cellular processes and men's overall health.
oyster.fullDescription:
Oysters are not just a popular seafood; they are also a source of many important nutrients, all of which play a role in the body's processes, from building and repairing cells to immune function and overall health.

One of the nutrients that draws particular attention to oysters is zinc, an essential mineral that the body cannot produce on its own. It is involved in the activity of a large number of enzymes, protein synthesis, cell division and the normal function of the immune system. Zinc also plays a role in reproductive processes and normal hormone function, making it one of the nutrients of importance to men's health.

Oysters also contain vitamin B12 and iron, which are involved in red blood cell formation and the transport of oxygen to tissues, while selenium is a component of certain enzymes involved in the body's defence against oxidative stress. Protein and amino acids are important for building and repairing tissue and for maintaining normal muscle function.
oyster.howItWorks:
Oysters and their mechanisms in the body
1. Cellular and immune function
Oysters are a seafood containing protein, amino acids and several important minerals that the body uses in the formation and function of immune cells, particularly zinc and selenium, which play a role in cellular function and in the defence against oxidative stress. Adequate intake of these nutrients therefore plays an important part in maintaining normal immune function.
2. The reproductive system and male hormones
Oysters have attracted interest in men's nutrition because they contain nutrients involved in reproductive function, especially zinc, which plays a role in sperm production and the maintenance of normal testosterone levels.
3. Muscles and tissue repair
Once protein from oysters has been digested and absorbed, the body can use it to build muscle protein, repair tissue and support cellular function.
oyster.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of oysters
Oysters can be consumed and processed in many forms, both as ordinary food and as extracts used as ingredients in dietary supplements. Each form differs in its characteristics and nutritional composition, as follows:
• Fresh or cooked oyster meat: commonly eaten as food; thorough cooking helps reduce the risk from pathogens
• Dried oyster meat: dehydrated to extend shelf life and used as a food ingredient
• Oyster powder: made from oyster meat that has been dried and ground into a powder
• Oyster extract: produced through an extraction process to obtain certain groups of compounds from oyster meat
• Dietary supplements: use oyster extract as an ingredient, possibly combined with other vitamins or minerals
oyster.scientificEvidence:
1. Nutritional value and the immune system
A review by Negara et al. (2022), which compiled 37 studies on the Pacific oyster (Crassostrea gigas), found that oyster meat contains protein, essential amino acids, glycogen, fatty acids and a wide range of minerals. In addition, compounds isolated from oysters showed antioxidant and immunomodulatory properties in some studies.
However, most of the evidence comes from laboratory experiments, so it cannot be concluded that eating oysters directly boosts immunity in humans.
2. Studies on the male reproductive system
Li et al. (2020) studied oyster peptides and oyster powder in male mice with reproductive damage induced by cyclophosphamide, tracking hormonal markers and the condition of testicular tissue. The study found that the group given oyster peptides showed favourable changes in some markers, including androgen levels and oxidative stress in the tissue.
However, this was an animal study, so effects on hormones, fertility or sexual performance in humans cannot yet be confirmed.
3. Studies on muscle strength
Lee (2022) conducted a trial in 54 adults aged 50–78 years in which the test group took 1,200 mg of fermented oyster extract per day for 12 weeks together with walking exercise, compared with a placebo group.
The study found that muscle strength and muscle mass did not increase significantly compared with the control group. Although the extract contains interesting amino acids and compounds, the results therefore do not yet support claims that oyster extract directly increases muscle mass or strength.
This information is provided to educate about oysters and is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating any disease.
oyster.safetyInformation:
• People who are allergic to shellfish or molluscan seafood should avoid products containing oyster ingredients.
• Raw or undercooked oysters may contain Vibrio and other pathogens, so they should be cooked thoroughly before eating, especially by people with liver disease or weakened immunity.
• Excessive intake of zinc from dietary supplements over a long period may interfere with copper absorption and cause side effects.
• Pregnant and breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare professional before using concentrated extracts, as product-specific safety data may be limited.
keyFunctions: A natural food source of zinc, which is involved in the normal function of the immune system
Contains zinc, which is essential for protein synthesis and cell division
Contains minerals involved in the body's normal reproductive processes
Contains vitamin B12, which is essential for red blood cell formation and nervous system function
Contains protein and several minerals that form part of a balanced diet

niacin.shortDescription: Niacin, or vitamin B3, plays an important role in the body's energy-yielding processes as a component in the formation of substances called NAD and NADP, which help cells use nutrients from carbohydrates, proteins and fats in various processes. Niacin also contributes to the maintenance of normal mucous membranes of the digestive tract, normal skin and normal nervous system function.
niacin.fullDescription:
The foods we eat every day, whether rice, meat or fat, are all important sources of energy for the body. But having nutrients in the body does not mean that cells can use them immediately, because they must still go through many steps of chemical conversion. One of the vitamins involved in these processes is niacin, or vitamin B3.

Niacin is a water-soluble vitamin belonging to the B-complex group and is found in a wide variety of foods, especially meat, fish, poultry, legumes and certain grains. In the body, niacin is the precursor for two important coenzymes: NAD (Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide) and NADP (Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide Phosphate).

The interest in niacin is not limited to energy-yielding processes; it is also involved in nervous system function and in maintaining normal skin and mucous membranes of the digestive tract, which is why the body needs an adequate intake of this vitamin.
niacin.howItWorks:
Niacin and its mechanisms in the body
1. Converting nutrients into energy
When we eat, the body breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and fats into substances that cells can use. Niacin is a component in the formation of NAD, which helps accept and donate electrons in the chemical reactions involved in producing energy within cells.
In other words, niacin does not provide energy as food does, but it is one of the nutrients that help the process of using energy from food proceed normally.
2. Maintaining normal skin and mucous membranes of the digestive tract
Skin cells and the cells lining the digestive tract are continuously renewed and repaired. These processes require energy and many steps of biochemical reactions in which NAD and NADP are involved. Adequate niacin intake is therefore part of maintaining the normal function of these cells.
3. Involvement in nervous system function
Nerve cells need energy to maintain cellular balance and to send signals to one another, so niacin is important through the role of NAD in energy production and cellular function. In addition, NAD is involved in the repair of genetic material and in regulating the activity of certain proteins within cells.
niacin.uniqueProperties:
Food sources of niacin
• Chicken and turkey
• Tuna and salmon
• Beef and liver
• Peanuts
• Certain mushrooms
• Whole grains
niacin.scientificEvidence:
1. Evidence on energy use from nutrients
Information from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) states that niacin is the precursor of NAD and NADP, coenzymes involved in more than 400 chemical reactions in the body, including the conversion of nutrients into energy.
This role is a recognised nutritional function, but it does not mean that niacin supplementation in people who already get enough vitamin B3 will further increase energy or strength.
2. Evidence on the skin and mucous membranes of the digestive tract
Severe niacin deficiency can cause pellagra, whose main symptoms involve the skin, the digestive system and the nervous system. Adequate niacin intake is therefore important for maintaining the normal function of these tissues.
However, evidence on correcting a vitamin deficiency cannot be used to conclude that taking additional niacin will directly improve the skin of people who are not deficient.
3. Evidence on nervous system function
Niacin plays an important role in the energy production of nerve cells and in the function of NAD, which is involved in various processes within cells.
Although severe niacin deficiency may affect the nervous system, there is not yet sufficient clinical evidence that niacin supplementation in people who already have adequate nutrition will improve memory, concentration or learning ability.
4. Studies on high-dose niacin
The AIM-HIGH and HPS2-THRIVE clinical trials studied high-dose nicotinic acid to evaluate its effects on cardiovascular health in at-risk patients. They found no clear additional benefit on major cardiovascular outcomes when used alongside certain standard treatments, while adverse effects increased.
These studies used niacin at therapeutic drug doses, which differ from the amounts normally obtained from food or ordinary dietary supplements, so their results should not be generalised to niacin in all doses and all forms.
This information is provided to educate about niacin and is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating any disease.
niacin.safetyInformation:
• High doses of nicotinic acid may cause skin redness, flushing, itching or discomfort.
• High intakes of niacin from dietary supplements or medicines may affect the liver, blood sugar levels and uric acid levels.
• People with liver disease, diabetes or gout, or who take regular medication, should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking high-dose niacin supplements.
• High-dose niacin should not be used to self-manage blood lipid levels without medical supervision.
keyFunctions: Contributes to the maintenance of normal mucous membranes of the digestive tract and normal skin
Contributes to normal energy-yielding metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats
Contributes to normal functioning of the nervous system

astragalus.shortDescription: Astragalus (known in Thai as Pak Kee or Aung Kee) is a herbal plant of the legume family whose root has a long history of use in traditional Chinese medicine. The root contains several groups of natural compounds, including polysaccharides, astragalosides and flavonoids, which have been studied for their relationship with cellular function, the immune system and antioxidant processes.
astragalus.fullDescription:
Astragalus (Astragalus membranaceus), known in Chinese as Huang Qi, is a herbal plant native to East Asia. The part most commonly used is the root, which is usually dried and cut into thin slices. In the past, astragalus was an ingredient in soups and Chinese herbal formulas, before being developed into powder and extract raw materials for today's dietary supplements.

What makes astragalus root interesting is the diversity of its natural constituents: more than 100 compounds have been identified, covering polysaccharides, saponins, flavonoids and amino acids, in particular Astragalus Polysaccharides (APS) and Astragaloside IV, key compounds whose biological properties have been studied in many areas.

Building on traditional herbal knowledge, modern science has extended the study of astragalus to cellular-level mechanisms, including communication between immune cells, oxidative processes and blood vessel function.
astragalus.howItWorks:
Astragalus and its mechanisms in the body
1. The immune system and communication between cells
The immune system relies on communication between many types of cells to regulate the body's responses. The polysaccharides in astragalus have been studied for their interactions with immune cells such as macrophages and lymphocytes, as well as the production of cytokines, proteins that act as signals between cells.
2. Oxidative balance within cells
During normal metabolism, the body continuously produces free radicals. The flavonoids and astragalosides in astragalus have therefore been studied in biological models to understand the interactions between these plant compounds and the antioxidant mechanisms within cells.
3. Function of the cells lining the blood vessels
The cells lining the blood vessels play a role in regulating the constriction and relaxation of blood vessels through several signalling molecules, one of which is nitric oxide. Laboratory studies of Astragaloside IV have covered these signalling mechanisms, which form the basis for studying astragalus in the context of heart and circulatory health.
astragalus.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of astragalus
Dried astragalus root is commonly used as an ingredient in soups, herbal teas and Chinese herbal formulas.
Astragalus powder is made from root that has been dried and finely ground, retaining several groups of constituents of the original raw material.
Astragalus extract is produced through an extraction process that isolates certain groups of compounds from the root.
Standardised astragalus extract is an extract with a specified content of certain key compounds, such as polysaccharides or Astragaloside IV.
astragalus.scientificEvidence:
1. Astragalus and the immune response
A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 19 human studies with a total of 1,094 participants to evaluate the relationship between astragalus use and immune markers. It found changes in some markers, such as cytokine levels and the proportions of immune cells.
However, most of the studies analysed were small and differed in their study methods, so the findings are not yet sufficient to confirm that taking astragalus can boost immunity or prevent illness in the general population.
2. Astragalus polysaccharides and their biological properties
A review article published in the journal Chinese Herbal Medicines in 2025 compiled data on the structure, extraction methods and biological properties of polysaccharides from astragalus, explaining that differences in molecular structure and extraction methods are key factors that may affect the properties of the resulting compounds.
This review helps explain that, even though the polysaccharides come from the same plant, their biological properties may differ depending on the production process, and further human studies are still needed.
3. Astragalosides, flavonoids and cellular-level function
A 2023 review examined data on flavonoids, saponins and polysaccharides from astragalus, covering both how these compounds are produced within the plant and the biological properties found in experiments, particularly mechanisms related to oxidative balance, the immune response and the cardiovascular system.
This information provides a basis for developing future clinical research, but it cannot yet be used to confirm the effectiveness of taking astragalus in daily life.
*This information is provided to educate about astragalus and is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating any disease.
astragalus.safetyInformation:
People with autoimmune diseases should avoid taking astragalus, as it may affect immune system function.
Astragalus may interact with immunosuppressant drugs. People who take regular medication should consult a doctor or pharmacist before using products containing astragalus.
Pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid dietary supplements containing astragalus, as safety data are still insufficient.
keyFunctions: Contains Astragalus Polysaccharides (APS), which have been studied for their effects on the immune response
Contains Astragaloside IV, which has been studied for its relationship with cellular and blood vessel function
Contains flavonoids, which have been studied for their antioxidant properties

vitamin-e.shortDescription: Vitamin E is a fat-soluble vitamin that plays an important role in protecting cells from oxidative stress and is also involved in the normal function of the immune system. Vitamin E is found in vegetable oils, nuts, seeds and certain vegetables.
vitamin-e.fullDescription:
When people talk about vitamin E, many think of skincare products or antioxidants, but the key role of this vitamin takes place at a level far smaller than the skin: the cell membrane, the structure that encloses each cell and maintains the environment inside the body's cells.

Vitamin E is a group of fat-soluble nutrients comprising 8 natural forms, divided into 4 tocopherols and 4 tocotrienols. Alpha-tocopherol is the form that the human body mainly maintains and uses to meet its vitamin E requirements.

What makes vitamin E special is its ability to act as an antioxidant in lipid-rich areas, especially cell membranes, which contain fatty acids that may be affected by oxidation. Vitamin E therefore contributes to protecting these lipids, supporting normal cellular function, immune function and communication between cells.
vitamin-e.howItWorks:
Vitamin E and its mechanisms in the body
1. Protecting the lipids in cell membranes
Cell membranes are made up of several types of lipids, especially unsaturated fatty acids that are sensitive to oxidation. Vitamin E can act as an antioxidant by helping to stop the chain reactions that may damage these lipids, and so contributes to maintaining the integrity of cell membranes.
2. Working together with other antioxidants
When vitamin E acts against oxidation, its chemical structure changes. Vitamin C and other antioxidant systems in the body can take part in converting vitamin E back to its active form. This mechanism reflects the fact that many antioxidants work together rather than in complete isolation.
3. Involvement in immune function
Vitamin E is involved in the function of immune cells, including maintaining the condition of cell membranes and signalling between cells. Adequate vitamin E intake is therefore important for the normal function of the immune system.
vitamin-e.uniqueProperties:
Food sources of vitamin E
• Sunflower seeds and sunflower oil
• Almonds and hazelnuts
• Wheat germ oil
• Certain vegetable oils, such as safflower oil
• Spinach and broccoli
• Avocado
vitamin-e.scientificEvidence:
1. Studies on protecting cells from oxidative stress
Vitamin E is recognised as a fat-soluble antioxidant, particularly alpha-tocopherol, which helps protect the fatty acids in cell membranes from oxidation.
Information from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) states that vitamin E is an essential nutrient that plays a role in immune function and various processes within cells. However, high intakes of vitamin E from dietary supplements have not consistently shown additional health benefits in clinical trials.
2. Studies on skin health
Vitamin E is a component of the skin's antioxidant system, and its role in protecting the lipids in skin cells from oxidation, as well as its interaction with vitamin C, has been studied.
However, clinical evidence on taking vitamin E orally to improve the appearance of the skin, reduce wrinkles or slow skin ageing is not yet sufficient to clearly confirm its effectiveness, especially in people who already get enough vitamin E from food.
3. Studies on the immune system
A trial by Meydani et al. (1997) in healthy older adults found that vitamin E supplementation at a defined dose was associated with changes in certain markers of the immune response.
However, this result does not mean that vitamin E supplementation will help reduce the likelihood of infection in all populations, as other trials have produced different results, and changes in immune markers do not always equal clinical benefit.
4. Studies on long-term health
The SELECT trial, which studied more than 35,000 men, found that vitamin E supplementation at 400 IU per day, in the form used in the trial, was associated with an increased risk of prostate cancer compared with placebo during follow-up.
This finding shows that high intakes of vitamin E from dietary supplements are not always beneficial and may carry risks different from normal vitamin E intake through food.
This information is provided to educate about vitamin E and is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating any disease.
vitamin-e.safetyInformation:
• Taking high doses of supplemental vitamin E may increase the risk of bleeding, especially when used together with anticoagulant or antiplatelet medicines.
• People with fat malabsorption disorders may be at risk of vitamin E deficiency and should be assessed by a healthcare professional.
keyFunctions: Vitamin E contributes to the protection of cells from free radicals
Vitamin E contributes to antioxidant processes
Involved in the normal function of the immune system
Involved in cell signalling and cellular function

pine-bark-extract.nameTh: สารสกัดเปลือกสน
pine-bark-extract.shortDescription: Pine bark extract is obtained from the bark of certain pine species and is rich in natural polyphenols, especially procyanidins, which have antioxidant properties related to skin health, cellular function and the vascular system.
pine-bark-extract.fullDescription:
Pine bark extract is a natural extract obtained from the bark of certain pine species. Pine bark contains several important compounds, especially polyphenols such as procyanidins, catechin and epicatechin, which have notable antioxidant properties.

Pine bark is also associated with vascular processes, particularly the function of the vascular endothelium and nitric oxide, which plays a part in regulating the dilation of blood vessels. Certain compounds in pine bark are also associated with the body's natural inflammatory response processes.

Another area of interest is skin health: certain pine bark extract formulas have also been studied for their relationship with skin hydration, elasticity and processes related to collagen and hyaluronic acid.
pine-bark-extract.howItWorks:
Pine bark and its mechanisms in the body
1. Protecting cells from oxidative stress
Pine bark extract contains polyphenols that have been studied for their ability to react with free radicals and their relationship with the systems that regulate oxidative balance within cells. Laboratory experiments have found that certain compounds may affect these processes.
2. The vascular system and endothelial function
Certain pine bark extract formulas have been studied in relation to the function of the endothelium, the layer of cells lining the inside of blood vessels, particularly processes involving nitric oxide, which plays a role in regulating the dilation of blood vessels.
3. The skin and tissue structure
Pine bark extract has attracted interest in studies of processes related to collagen and hyaluronic acid, key components of skin structure. Some studies have found changes in skin hydration, elasticity and dark spots after the extract was taken.
pine-bark-extract.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of pine bark extract
• Dried pine bark: raw material from the bark of pine trees that has been dried for use in processing or extraction
• Powdered pine bark extract: extract that has been dried and ground into a powder for use as an ingredient in products
• Standardised extract: extract with a specified content of certain groups of key compounds according to the manufacturer's specifications
• Combination dietary supplements: pine bark extract used together with vitamins, minerals or other plant extracts
pine-bark-extract.scientificEvidence:
1. Studies on skin hydration and elasticity
A study in 112 women with signs of photoaged skin examined oral intake of French maritime pine bark extract for 12 weeks and found that skin condition scores and pigmentation levels of dark spots decreased significantly on some measures.
However, the study did not have a placebo group for direct comparison, so it cannot yet be confirmed that the observed effects were due to the extract alone.
2. Studies on vascular function
A systematic review published in 2025, pooling 27 randomised trials with a total of 1,685 participants, found that the use of pine bark extract was associated with changes in some markers, such as blood pressure, blood sugar levels and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, but found no significant differences in other markers, such as high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol and triglycerides.
The findings therefore reflect a scientific possibility rather than confirmation of the effectiveness of every extract formula.
3. Studies on skin pigmentation processes
A randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial in 44 women studied the use of the pine bark extract Pycnogenol® together with standard skincare products for 60 days and found that the group receiving the extract showed greater changes in skin pigmentation scores than the placebo group.
However, this result comes from a study of a specific extract formula used together with other skincare methods, so conclusions cannot be drawn for pine bark extracts in general.
This information is provided to educate about pine bark and is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating any disease.
pine-bark-extract.safetyInformation:
• Taking pine bark extract may cause stomach discomfort, nausea, dizziness or headache in some people.
• People taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet medicines should consult a doctor or pharmacist before use.
• People taking blood-sugar-lowering or blood-pressure-lowering medicines should consult a healthcare professional before taking concentrated extracts.
• Pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid using concentrated extracts without advice from a specialist.
keyFunctions: A source of polyphenol compounds, especially procyanidins
Its antioxidant properties have been studied at the laboratory level
There is research on oxidative stress and cellular responses
Has attracted interest in studies of vascular function
Has been studied for its relationship with skin structure and condition in humans

zinc.shortDescription: Zinc is an essential mineral that the body cannot produce on its own. It plays a role in enzyme activity, protein synthesis, cell division and the normal function of the immune system, making it one of the minerals the body needs to obtain in adequate amounts from food.
zinc.fullDescription:
Zinc is a mineral the body needs only in small amounts, yet it is involved in many biological processes, from the growth and development of the body to cellular function and the balance of various systems.

The body cannot produce zinc on its own, so it must be obtained from food, such as oysters, meat, eggs, dairy products, legumes and certain grains. The absorption of zinc may vary depending on the food source and the composition of the meal.

In addition to zinc from food, zinc is also available in dietary supplement forms such as zinc gluconate, zinc citrate and zinc amino acid chelate, which differ in chemical structure and the amount of zinc they provide. The choice of supplement should therefore take into account need and total zinc intake.
zinc.howItWorks:
What does zinc do?
• Enzyme activity: zinc is involved in the activity of a large number of enzymes in the body
• Protein and genetic material synthesis: plays a role in the synthesis of proteins and DNA
• Cell division and growth: is a key component in the development and repair of tissues
• The immune system: is involved in the development and normal function of immune cells
• Taste and smell: is involved in the normal function of the senses of taste and smell
Zinc and its mechanisms in the body
Once the body absorbs zinc into the bloodstream and transports it to cells, zinc acts as an essential cofactor for the activity of hundreds of enzymes in the body. It binds to the catalytic sites of these enzymes, helping the biochemical processes and nutrient metabolism within cells to proceed normally and continuously.
Beyond its role in enzymes, zinc also has an important structural role at the molecular level, especially as the core of a group of proteins called "zinc fingers", which help stabilise protein structure and work with genetic material to regulate gene expression. As a result, the transmission of genetic information, cell division and cell growth proceed according to their natural cycle.
At the same time, zinc also acts as a cellular signalling agent, helping to maintain the balance of cellular function in various systems of the body.
zinc.uniqueProperties:
Food sources of zinc
• Oysters and shellfish, such as crab and shrimp
• Lean meats, such as beef, pork and lamb, and poultry such as chicken breast or turkey
• Egg yolks and dairy products, such as fresh milk, cheese and yoghurt
• Seeds, such as pumpkin seeds, sesame seeds and sunflower seeds
• Nuts and dried beans, such as cashews, almonds, chickpeas and red kidney beans
• Whole grains, such as oats, quinoa, brown rice and wholewheat bread
• Dark chocolate with 70% cocoa or more, and cocoa powder
zinc.scientificEvidence:
• Nutritional data and research support zinc as an essential mineral for enzyme activity, the immune system, the synthesis of genetic material and the processes of cell growth.
• Forms in supplements: the NIH reports that zinc citrate and zinc gluconate are absorbed to a similar extent, and it is not yet clear which form is better. Comparative data specifically for the amino acid chelate form are still limited.
• The natural role of zinc in the body does not mean that taking zinc supplements will improve everyone's health or provide additional benefits, especially for people who already get enough zinc from food.
This page is provided for information about zinc's nutritional role only and is not advice for treating or preventing any disease.
zinc.safetyInformation:
• Zinc is an essential mineral, but excessive intake may cause nausea, stomach pain or disturb the balance of other minerals, especially copper, when high amounts of zinc are taken continuously over a long period.
• Zinc supplements may also interact with certain medicines, such as some groups of antibiotics. People who take regular medication, have underlying health conditions or are considering taking several dietary supplements together should consult a doctor or pharmacist before use.
keyFunctions: Zinc contributes to the normal function of the immune system
Zinc contributes to normal DNA synthesis
Zinc contributes to the maintenance of normal skin, hair and nails
Zinc contributes to the maintenance of normal vision
Zinc contributes to the protection of cells from oxidative stress
Zinc contributes to normal protein synthesis

selenium.shortDescription: Selenium plays a role in the activity of enzymes involved in protecting cells from oxidative stress, as well as in the normal function of the immune system and the thyroid gland. It can be obtained from a wide variety of foods.
selenium.fullDescription:
Selenium is a trace mineral, a mineral the body needs only in small amounts. Although the requirement is small, selenium is a component of a specific group of proteins called selenoproteins, which play important roles in cellular processes.

These proteins are involved in regulating oxidative balance in the body, thyroid hormone function and the normal function of the immune system.

The body obtains selenium from foods such as fish, seafood, meat, eggs and grains. The selenium content of plant foods may vary depending on the mineral content of the soil in which they are grown.
selenium.howItWorks:
What does selenium do?
• A shield for cells: is a component of enzymes that help maintain the balance of oxidative reactions within cells
• Supports the thyroid: works with enzymes that help convert thyroid hormones into their active form
• Supports immunity: contributes to the natural function and responses of immune cells
• A component of key proteins: is incorporated into selenoproteins that drive various mechanisms in the body
Selenium and its mechanisms in the body
Selenium that enters the body is used as a key component in building specialised proteins called selenoproteins, a major group of proteins that regulate biochemical reactions and keep cellular-level functions working normally.
One of the key mechanisms of this group of proteins is serving as a main component of enzymes in the antioxidant system, such as glutathione peroxidase, which helps deal with free radicals that form naturally during energy metabolism, as well as working with enzymes in thyroid tissue to maintain the balance of thyroid hormone function.
The production and combined action of these proteins is a fundamental mechanism that helps the various systems within cells maintain balance and function normally from day to day.
selenium.uniqueProperties:
Food sources of selenium
• Seafood and marine fish: short mackerel, tuna (both fresh and canned), sardines, shrimp, crab, cockles and oysters
• Meat and offal: pork, beef, chicken, as well as pork liver and chicken liver
• Eggs and dairy products: chicken eggs, duck eggs, cow's milk and yoghurt
• Grains and rice: brown rice, Riceberry rice, Hom Mali (jasmine) rice and oats
• Nuts and seeds: sunflower seeds, cashews, peanuts, white and black sesame seeds
• Mushrooms and local vegetables: shiitake mushrooms, straw mushrooms, Indian oyster mushrooms, garlic and asparagus
selenium.scientificEvidence:
• The role of selenoproteins: selenium is a component of proteins involved in regulating oxidative balance, thyroid hormone function and other biological processes.
• The immune system: selenium plays a role in the function of immune cells, but the evidence does not confirm that selenium supplementation in people who already get enough will always improve immunity.
• Selenium from yeast: is a source of selenium used in nutritional studies and dietary supplements. However, research outcomes depend on the form of the compound, the dose and the population studied.
This page is provided for information about selenium's nutritional role only and is not advice for treating or preventing any disease.
selenium.safetyInformation:
• Excessive selenium intake, especially from taking several dietary supplements together, may cause nausea, digestive disturbances, hair loss or brittle nails.
• Continuous intake of high amounts of selenium may be harmful to health, so the recommended amount should not be exceeded without advice from a specialist.
• People with underlying health conditions, who take regular medication or are considering taking several dietary supplements together should consult a doctor or pharmacist before use.
• People who are allergic to yeast should check the source and allergen information of products that use selenium-enriched yeast before consumption.

vitamin-b6.shortDescription: Vitamin B6 plays an important role in nervous system function, red blood cell formation and the immune system. It is also involved in the metabolism of homocysteine, an amino acid that has attracted interest in studies of vascular health.
vitamin-b6.fullDescription:
Vitamin B6 is one of the B vitamins that the body needs to obtain from food. It serves as a component of coenzymes involved in more than 100 biochemical reactions, especially the metabolism of proteins and amino acids, as well as nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

A key feature of vitamin B6 is its involvement in the synthesis of neurotransmitters such as serotonin, dopamine and GABA, substances involved in communication between nerve cells. At the same time, vitamin B6 also takes part in the metabolism of homocysteine, a substance that has been associated with heart and vascular health in some research.

In addition, vitamin B6 is essential for the normal function of the immune system, being involved in the activity of immune cells and the production of certain substances used in the body's responses.
vitamin-b6.howItWorks:
Vitamin B6 and its mechanisms in the body
1. Homocysteine metabolism and vascular health
Vitamin B6 takes part in converting homocysteine into other substances through amino acid metabolism, working together with enzymes that require vitamin B6 in its active form.
2. Red blood cell formation and energy metabolism
Vitamin B6 is also involved in the synthesis of heme, a component of haemoglobin in red blood cells, making it important for normal red blood cell formation. It also acts as a coenzyme in the metabolism of amino acids and glycogen, so that the body can use nutrients in energy production normally.
3. Neurotransmitter synthesis and brain function
Vitamin B6 in the form of pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) acts as a coenzyme in the synthesis of several neurotransmitters, such as serotonin, dopamine and GABA, which are involved in communication between nerve cells and the regulation of nervous system function.
4. Immune system function
Vitamin B6 is involved in amino acid metabolism and the production of substances needed for the function of immune cells. Vitamin B6 deficiency may affect some aspects of the immune response.
vitamin-b6.uniqueProperties:
Food sources of vitamin B6
• Fish, such as salmon and tuna
• Meat and poultry, such as chicken
• Chickpeas and certain legumes
• Potatoes and certain starchy vegetables
• Bananas
• Cereals or foods fortified with vitamin B6
vitamin-b6.scientificEvidence:
• Vitamin B6 has a clear biochemical role in amino acid metabolism, neurotransmitter synthesis and nervous system function.
• Studies confirm that vitamin B6 deficiency may affect red blood cell formation and immune system function.
• Vitamin B6 is involved in homocysteine metabolism, but clinical trials do not yet support the use of vitamin B6 to prevent cardiovascular disease in the general population.
• Research on brain function, mood and memory has not yet been able to confirm a benefit of vitamin B6 supplementation in people with adequate nutrient intake.
This page is provided for information about composition and nutritional role only and is not advice for treating or preventing any disease.
vitamin-b6.safetyInformation:
• Continuous intake of high doses of vitamin B6 may cause peripheral neuropathy, such as numbness or impaired balance.
• Check the total amount of vitamin B6 from all dietary supplements taken, especially when using B-complex vitamins or several supplement products together.
• Vitamin B6 may interact with certain medicines, such as levodopa when not used with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor, and certain anticonvulsants.

zinc-gluconate.shortDescription: Zinc gluconate is one of the forms of zinc used in dietary supplements.
zinc-gluconate.fullDescription: Zinc is a nutrient the body needs. The amount of elemental zinc per serving matters more than the total weight of the compound.
zinc-gluconate.howItWorks: Zinc is involved in immune function and in normal DNA and protein synthesis.
zinc-gluconate.uniqueProperties: Zinc comes in several forms, such as gluconate, acetate and sulfate. It is not yet clear that any one form is better in every case.
zinc-gluconate.scientificEvidence: Total intake from food and supplements should be assessed, rather than choosing based on the name of the form alone.
zinc-gluconate.safetyInformation:
Excessive intake may cause nausea, and high intake over a long period may lead to low copper levels.

This information is for educational purposes and is not medical advice. People who are pregnant, breastfeeding, have underlying health conditions or are taking medication should consult a doctor or pharmacist before using dietary supplements.
